claim: The complete Liverpool SPN catalogue contains 6674 individual SPNs from 2215 participants.
source: Here we report how we have made a total of 6674 individual SPNs from 2215 participants publicly available, along with data extraction and visualization tools (https://osf.io/2sncj/).
evidence: The abstract directly states the number of recordings and participants in the catalogue.

claim: Humans can detect visual symmetry very efficiently.
source: Many natural and man-made objects are symmetrical, and humans can detect visual symmetry very efficiently (Bertamini et al., 2018; Treder, 2010; Tyler, 1995; Wagemans, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The sustained posterior negativity (SPN) is a brain response to visual symmetry.
source: Since 2011, we have been using EEG in experiments at the University of Liverpool to measure a brain response to visual symmetry called the sustained posterior negativity (SPN; see Box 1 and Figure 1).
evidence: The text defines the SPN as a brain response to visual symmetry based on the authors' research program.

claim: By October 2020, 40 SPN projects had been completed, with 17 published and 23 unpublished or under review.
source: By October 2020 we had completed 40 SPN projects: 17 of these had been published, and the remaining 23 were either unpublished or under review.
evidence: The text explicitly states the number of projects and their publication status.

claim: SPN amplitude increases with the proportion of symmetry in the image.
source: Note that SPN amplitude increases (that is, becomes more negative) with the proportion of symmetry in the image. In this experiment, the SPN increased from ~0 to –3.5 microvolts as symmetry increased from 20% to 100%. Adapted from Figures 1, 3 and 4 in Makin et al., 2020c.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from a specific experiment and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The COVID pandemic stopped all EEG testing in March 2020.
source: The COVID pandemic stopped all our EEG testing in March 2020, and we used this crisis/opportunity to organize and catalogue our existing data.
evidence: The text directly states when testing stopped due to the pandemic.

claim: The complete Liverpool SPN catalogue is publicly available at https://osf.io/2sncj/.
source: The data from all 40 of our SPN projects are now available in a public repository called "The complete Liverpool SPN catalogue" (available at https://osf.io/2sncj/; see Box 2 and Figure 2).
evidence: The text explicitly provides the URL for the public repository.

claim: Publication bias leads to systematic overestimation of effect sizes in meta-analysis.
source: This publication bias leads to systematic overestimation of effect sizes in meta-analysis (Brysbaert, 2019; Button et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research on publication bias.

claim: Unpublished SPNs were weaker than published SPNs by a mean difference of 0.354 microvolts.
source: The unpublished SPNs were weaker than the published SPNs (mean difference = 0.354 microvolts [95% CI=0.162–0.546], t (218.003)=3.640, P<.001, equal variance not assumed).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the catalogue data.

claim: Published SPNs came from experiments with smaller sample sizes than unpublished SPNs.
source: Furthermore, the published SPNs came from experiments with smaller sample sizes (mean sample sizes = 23.40 vs 29.49, P<.001, Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of sample sizes.

claim: The weighted mean amplitude of published SPNs was –1.138 microvolts.
source: The weighted mean amplitude of the published SPNs was –1.138 microvolts [95% CI = –1.290; –0.986].
evidence: The claim is based on meta-analysis of published SPNs.

claim: The weighted mean amplitude of unpublished SPNs was –0.801 microvolts.
source: This was reduced to –0.801 microvolts [–0.914; –0.689] for the unpublished SPNs, and to –0.954 microvolts [–1.049; –0.860] for all SPNs.
evidence: The claim is based on meta-analysis of unpublished SPNs.

claim: The weighted mean amplitude of all SPNs was –0.954 microvolts.
source: This was reduced to –0.801 microvolts [–0.914; –0.689] for the unpublished SPNs, and to –0.954 microvolts [–1.049; –0.860] for all SPNs.
evidence: The claim is based on meta-analysis of all SPNs in the catalogue.

claim: The funnel plot for published SPNs shows asymmetry, which is a fingerprint of publication bias.
source: The funnel plot for the published SPNs (Figure 3A; bottom panel) is not symmetrically tapered (less accurate measures near the base of the funnel are skewed leftwards). This is a textbook fingerprint of publication bias.
evidence: The claim is based on visual inspection of the funnel plot and comparison to known patterns of publication bias.

claim: Funnel asymmetry was significant for unpublished SPNs and all SPNs, indicating publication bias cannot be the sole explanation.
source: However, the funnel asymmetry was still significant for the unpublished SPNs and for all SPNs, so publication bias cannot be the explanation (see Zwetsloot et al., 2017 for detailed analysis of funnel asymmetry).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of funnel plots and cited research on funnel asymmetry.

claim: P1 peak amplitude was essentially identical in published and unpublished work.
source: P1 peak was essentially identical in published and unpublished work (4.672 vs 4.686, t (195.11) = –0.067, P=.946; Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of P1 amplitudes.

claim: N1 trough was larger in published work than unpublished work.
source: However, the N1 trough was larger in published work (–8.736 vs. –7.155. t (183.61) = –5.636, P<.001; Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of N1 amplitudes.

claim: Publication bias is not a problem in the authors' SPN research.
source: However, we do not think publication bias is a problem in our SPN research.
evidence: The authors interpret their findings and conclude publication bias is not problematic for their work.

claim: Published and unpublished SPNs are from heterogeneous studies with different stimuli and tasks.
source: The published and unpublished SPNs are from heterogenous studies, with different stimuli and tasks.
evidence: The authors describe the nature of their dataset.

claim: The best estimate of mean SPN amplitude is –0.954 microvolts, which is far below zero.
source: Our best estimate of mean SPN amplitude (–0.954 microvolts) is far below zero [95% CI = –1.049; –0.860].
evidence: The claim is based on meta-analysis of all SPNs.

claim: An effect on the cusp of significance (P=.05) has only a 50% chance of successful replication.
source: The first misunderstanding is that an effect on the cusp of significance (P=.05) has a 95% chance of successful replication, when in fact the probability of successful replication is only 50% (power = 0.5).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical principles of power analysis.

claim: Median statistical power in cognitive neuroscience is estimated to be 0.21.
source: Indeed, one influential analysis estimated that median statistical power in cognitive neuroscience is just 0.21 (Button et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The conventional threshold for adequate statistical power is 0.8.
source: In stark contrast, the conventional threshold for adequate power is 0.8.
evidence: The claim is based on established statistical conventions.

claim: There is a nonlinear relationship between SPN amplitude and effect size dz.
source: Figure 4A shows the relationship between SPN amplitude and effect size dz. The larger (more negative) the SPN in microvolts, the larger dz. The curve tails off for strong SPNs, resulting in a nonlinear relationship.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the catalogue data and illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: A second order polynomial trendline fits the SPN amplitude-effect size relationship better than a first order linear trendline.
source: The second order polynomial trendline was a better fit than the first order linear trendline (see the supplementary polynomial regression analysis at https://osf.io/f2659/).
evidence: The claim is based on regression analysis comparing model fits.

claim: The average effect size dz for a 0.5 microvolt SPN is –0.469.
source: The average dz for a 0.5 microvolt SPN is –0.469.
evidence: The claim is based on the polynomial regression equation applied to the catalogue data.

claim: To have an 80% chance of finding a 0.5 microvolt SPN effect, a sample of 38 participants is needed.
source: Power analysis shows that to have an 80% chance of finding an effect of this size (P<.05, two tailed) we need a sample of 38 participants.
evidence: The claim is based on power analysis using the estimated effect size.

claim: The median sample size in the SPN catalogue is 24 participants.
source: In contrast, our median sample size is 24, which gives us an observed power of just 60%.
evidence: The claim is based on descriptive statistics of the catalogue.

claim: A median sample size of 24 gives an observed power of 60% for detecting a 0.5 microvolt SPN.
source: In contrast, our median sample size is 24, which gives us an observed power of just 60%.
evidence: The claim is based on power analysis using the median sample size.

claim: If a significant 0.5 microvolt SPN were replicated with the same sample size, there is a 40% chance of not finding the significant SPN again.
source: In other words, if we were to choose a significant 0.5 microvolt SPN and rerun the exact same experiment, there is a 100%–60%=40% chance we would not find the significant SPN again.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed power calculation.

claim: Only a third of the 249 SPNs are 0.5 microvolts or less.
source: Only a third of the 249 SPNs are 0.5 microvolts or less.
evidence: The claim is based on descriptive statistics of the catalogue.

claim: 9.2% of the 249 SPNs were not normally distributed according to the Shapiro-Wilk test.
source: Of the 249 SPNs, 9.2% were not normally distributed about the mean according to the Shapiro-Wilk test (8.4% according to Kolmogorov-Smirnov test).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical testing of normality in the catalogue data.

claim: For a significant binomial test with 24 participants, at least 18/24 (3/4) participants must show the directional effect.
source: Consider a typical 24 participant SPN: For a significant binomial test (P<.05, two tailed), we need at least 18/24=3/4 participants in the sample to show the directional effect (regular < random).
evidence: The claim is based on binomial test requirements.

claim: With 48 participants, only 32/48 (2/3) participants need to show the directional effect for a significant binomial test.
source: Next, consider doubling sample size to 48: We now need only 32/48=2/3 participants in the sample to show the directional effect.
evidence: The claim is based on binomial test requirements with larger sample size.

claim: Only 59% of grand-average SPNs were computed from samples where at least 3/4 of participants showed the directional effect.
source: Only 146 of the 249 grand-average SPNs (59%) were computed from a sample where at least 3/4 of the participants showed the directional effect.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of individual participant data in the catalogue.

claim: 73% of grand-average SPNs were from samples where at least 2/3 of participants showed the directional effect.
source: Meanwhile, 183 (73%) were from a sample where at least 2/3 of the participants showed the directional effect (blue horizontals in Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of individual participant data in the catalogue.

claim: Observed power was less than 0.8 in 15 of 40 representative ANOVA analyses.
source: Observed power was less than the desired 0.8 in 15 of 40 (Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is based on power analysis of ANOVA effects from the catalogue.

claim: Adding trials is an alternative way to increase statistical power in ERP research.
source: Another line of attack is to increase the number of trials per participant. Boudewyn et al., 2018 argue that adding trials is alternative way to increase statistical power in ERP research, even when split-half reliability is apparently near ceiling (as it is in SPN research: Makin et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research and reference to SPN reliability data.

claim: Increasing trials from 45 to 90 increased the probability of achieving a significant 0.5 microvolt ERP modulation from ~.54 to ~.89 in a sample of 24.
source: In one highly relevant analysis, Boudewyn et al., 2018 examined a within-participant 0.5 microvolt ERP modulation with a sample of 24 (our median sample). Increasing the number of trials from 45 to 90 increased the probability of achieving a significant effect from ~.54 to~.89 (see figure eight in Boudewyn et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is based on cited research findings.

claim: The mean sample size in 1,442 EEG articles from PubMed Central was 35.
source: A total of 1,442 sample sizes were obtained. Mean sample size was 35 (±22.97) and a median was 28.
evidence: The claim is based on text-mining analysis of published EEG research.

claim: The median sample size in 1,442 EEG articles from PubMed Central was 28.
source: A total of 1,442 sample sizes were obtained. Mean sample size was 35 (±22.97) and a median was 28.
evidence: The claim is based on text-mining analysis of published EEG research.

claim: The most commonly occurring sample size in EEG articles from PubMed Central was 20.
source: The most commonly occurring sample size was 20.
evidence: The claim is based on text-mining analysis of published EEG research.

claim: The mean sample size in 74 EEG datasets on OpenNeuro was 39.34.
source: We also extracted sample sizes from 74 EEG datasets on the OpenNeuro BIDS compliant repository. The mean sample size was 39.34 (±38.56), the median was 24, and the mode was again 20.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of publicly available EEG datasets.

claim: The median sample size in 74 EEG datasets on OpenNeuro was 24.
source: We also extracted sample sizes from 74 EEG datasets on the OpenNeuro BIDS compliant repository. The mean sample size was 39.34 (±38.56), the median was 24, and the mode was again 20.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of publicly available EEG datasets.

claim: Low statistical power is an obstacle to cumulative SPN research.
source: Low statistical power is an obstacle to cumulative SPN research.
evidence: The authors conclude based on their power analyses.

claim: P-hacking involves exploiting flexibility in the analysis pipeline to nudge effects over the threshold for statistical significance.
source: An effect that vibrates substantially is vulnerable to 'P-hacking': that is, exploiting flexibility in the analysis pipeline to nudge effects over the threshold for statistical significance (for example, P=.06 conveniently becomes P=.04, and the result is publishable).
evidence: The text defines P-hacking.

claim: Double dipping is a type of P-hacking where researchers select data after observing where something is happening, then run statistical analysis on this selection alone.
source: "Double dipping" is one particularly tempting type of P-hacking for cognitive neuroscientists because we typically have such large, multi-dimensional data sets (Kriegeskorte et al., 2009). Researchers can dip into a large dataset, observe where something is happening, then run statistical analysis on this data selection alone.
evidence: The text defines double dipping with citation to prior research.

claim: SPN amplitude is highly correlated across three alternative electrode clusters (Pearson's r ranged from .946 to .982).
source: Reassuringly, we found that SPN amplitude is highly correlated across clusters (Pearson's r ranged from .946 to .982, P<.001; Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis of SPNs computed with different electrode clusters.

claim: Vibration of SPN amplitude due to electrode choice is low.
source: This suggests vibration is low, and flexible electrode choice has not greatly influenced our SPN findings.
evidence: The authors infer from the high correlations across electrode clusters.

claim: The number of significant SPNs varies only slightly (169-177) across different electrode clusters.
source: The significant SPN count varies only slightly, between 169 and 177 (χ2 (3)=0.779, P=.854).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical testing of SPNs across different electrode clusters.

claim: Flexible electrode choice has not substantially inflated the number of significant SPNs.
source: We conclude that flexible electrode choice has not substantially inflated the number of significant SPNs in our research.
evidence: The authors conclude based on the similar significant SPN counts across clusters.

claim: 38 of 40 ANOVA effects were significant using the original electrode cluster, but this decreased with alternative clusters.
source: We applied the same reanalysis to our 40 representative ANOVA main effects and interactions. Here there is more cause for concern: 38 of the 40 effects were significant using the original electrode cluster, however this goes down to 33 with Cluster 1, 35 with Cluster 2, and to just 29 with Cluster 3 (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is based on reanalysis of ANOVA effects with different electrode clusters.

claim: Flexible electrode choice has significantly increased the number of significant SPN modulations.
source: Flexible electrode choice has thus significantly increased the number of significant SPN modulations (χ2 (3)=8.107, P=.044).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical testing of ANOVA effects across electrode clusters.

claim: Electrodes O1 and PO7 are most likely to capture the SPN over the left hemisphere.
source: Findings indicate that electrodes O1 and PO7 are most likely to capture the SPN over the left hemisphere, and O2 and PO8 are most likely to capture the SPN over the right hemisphere.
evidence: The claim is based on spatiotemporal clustering analysis of the catalogue data.

claim: Electrodes O2 and PO8 are most likely to capture the SPN over the right hemisphere.
source: Findings indicate that electrodes O1 and PO7 are most likely to capture the SPN over the left hemisphere, and O2 and PO8 are most likely to capture the SPN over the right hemisphere.
evidence: The claim is based on spatiotemporal clustering analysis of the catalogue data.

claim: SPN activity was mostly confined to the 200 to 1000ms window, extending somewhat to 1500ms.
source: Figure 7B shows activity was mostly confined to the 200 to 1000ms window, extending somewhat to 1500ms.
evidence: The claim is based on spatiotemporal clustering analysis illustrated in Figure 7B.

claim: There is a strong correlation between SPNs computed using spatiotemporal clustering and a priori electrode clusters (Pearson's r ranged from .719 to .746).
source: There was a strong correlation between this and SPN from each a priori cluster (Pearson's r ranged from .719 to .746, P<.001; Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis comparing spatiotemporal clustering results to a priori selections.

claim: 74% of published datasets yielded a significant spatiotemporal cluster, while only 57% of unpublished datasets did.
source: First, 74% of published data sets yielded a significant cluster, while the figure was only 57% for unpublished data (as of May 2022).
evidence: The claim is based on spatiotemporal clustering analysis of published vs unpublished data.

claim: Similar grand-average SPNs result from disparate EEGLAB and BESA preprocessing pipelines.
source: As seen in Figure 9, similar grand-average SPNs fall out at the end of these disparate pipelines.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of SPNs from 5 experiments processed with different software.

claim: Post-hoc selection of electrodes and time windows are weak points that can be exploited by P-hackers.
source: We conclude that post-hoc selection of electrodes and time windows are weak points that can be exploited by unscrupulous P-hackers.
evidence: The authors conclude based on their analyses of analytical flexibility.

claim: Earlier points in the preprocessing pipeline are less susceptible to P-hacking because changing them does not predictably increase or decrease the desired ERP effect.
source: Earlier points in the pipeline are less susceptible to P-hacking because changing them does not predictably increase or decrease the desired ERP effect.
evidence: The authors infer based on their pipeline comparison analysis.

claim: P-hacking is not a pervasive problem in SPN research, although some effects rely too heavily on post hoc data selection.
source: However, our assessment is that P-hacking is not a pervasive problem in SPN research, although some effects rely too heavily on post hoc data selection.
evidence: The authors conclude based on their comprehensive analysis of analytical flexibility.

claim: Most SPN effects could be recreated with a variety of justifiable analysis pipelines.
source: Reassuringly, we found most effects could be recreated with a variety of justifiable analysis pipelines: Data-driven and a priori approaches gave similar results, as did different EEGLAB and BESA pipelines.
evidence: The authors summarize their findings from multiple reanalysis approaches.

claim: HARKing is difficult to diagnose with reanalysis.
source: Unlike the other horses, HARKing and BARKing are difficult to diagnose with reanalysis, which is why this section is shorter than the previous sections.
evidence: The authors explain the limitation of their meta-scientific approach for assessing HARKing.

claim: Pre-registration of hypotheses is the main tool to fight HARKing.
source: The main tool to fight HARKing is online pre-registration of hypotheses (for example, on aspredicted.org or osf.io).
evidence: The authors recommend pre-registration based on established open science practices.

claim: Registered reports can abolish both HARKing and BARKing.
source: An even stricter approach is to use registered reports, where the introductions and methods are peer reviewed before data collection. This can abolish both HARKing and BARKing (Chambers, 2013; Munafò et al., 2017), but we have only just started with this.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research on registered reports.

claim: The 115 published SPNs were slightly stronger than the 134 unpublished ones.
source: As regards publication bias – the first horseman of irreproducibility – we found that the 115 published SPNs were slightly stronger than the 134 unpublished ones.
evidence: The authors summarize their findings on publication bias.

claim: There is no strong file drawer problem in the SPN research.
source: However, we are confident that there is no strong file drawer problem here.
evidence: The authors conclude based on their analysis of published vs unpublished SPNs.

claim: Reliable SPN research programs require larger samples than the typical sample size of 24.
source: Our most negative conclusion is that reliable SPN research programs require larger samples than those we typically obtain (38 participants are required to reliably measure –0.5 microvolt SPNs and our median sample size is 24).
evidence: The authors conclude based on their power analysis.

claim: It is possible to 'get by' while routinely conducting underpowered experiments without noticing a glaring problem.
source: It is evidently possible to 'get by' while routinely conducting underpowered experiments. One never notices a glaring problem: after all, underpowered research will often yield a lucky experiment with significant results, and this may support a new publication before moving on to the next topic.
evidence: The authors reflect on the implications of their power analysis findings.

claim: The costs of underpowered research might be masked by P-hacking.
source: The costs of underpowered research might be masked by the third horseman: P-hacking.
evidence: The authors speculate on the relationship between low power and P-hacking.

claim: Some SPN modulations were not robust to alternative electrode cluster selections.
source: However, some of our SPN modulations were not so robust, and we have relied on post hoc time windows.
evidence: The authors acknowledge limitations in their P-hacking analysis.

claim: Pre-registration is the best anti-HARKing tool.
source: Nevertheless, pre-registration is the best anti-HARKing tool, and we could have engaged with this earlier.
evidence: The authors recommend pre-registration based on established practices.

claim: It took more than a year to organize and catalogue all the SPN data.
source: It took more than a year to find all the SPN data, organize it, reformat it, produce uniform scripts, conduct rigorous double checks, and upload material to public databases.
evidence: The authors describe the effort required to create the catalogue.

claim: Creating the catalogue is anticipated to save far more than a year in terms of improved research efficiency.
source: However, we anticipate that it will save far more than a year in terms of improved research efficiency.
evidence: The authors speculate on the future benefits of the catalogue.

claim: Unpublished datasets now contribute to more reliable estimates of SPN effect size and power.
source: It is also satisfying that unpublished data sets are not merely lost. Instead, they are now contributing to more reliable estimates of SPN effect size and power.
evidence: The authors describe a benefit of the catalogue.

claim: No alternative activity could have been more beneficial for SPN research than creating the catalogue.
source: It is unlikely that any alternative activity could have been more beneficial for SPN research.
evidence: The authors express their opinion on the value of the catalogue.
